docs.title: Technology
docs.text:
Technology in Stellaris is divided into 3 research areas with each area corresponding with one of the research resources: Engineering, Physics and Society. Additionally, each of the ~400 techs belongs to one of 13 subcategories divided between the areas (most appearing pre-dominantly in one area though not exclusively).

The user interaction aspect utilizes a card shuffle approach rather than a traditional tech tree presentation, thereby introducing an element of semi-randomness into the system.

Each technology has a base cost which is modified by "Technology and Tradition Cost" (from galaxy settings set when starting a new game) and by empire size (the research cost is increased by 0.2% for each point of empire size above 100).

- Research areas & fields

There are three different main research areas in-game, with each area corresponding with one of the research resources. Additionally, each research area has multiple subcategories, for a total of 13 such subcategories, and every tech belongs to one of these subcategories.

The areas and their subcategories are as follows:

Physics Physics research
tech fields

Society Society research
tech fields

Engineering Engineering research

- Technology cards

Although the underlying technology system is based on the familiar tech tree structure, it does away with the traditional interaction/presentation in favor of the card shuffle approach. This injects a semi-random element into research, making it somewhat less predictable as well as less linear.

Whenever the player is prompted to initiate a research project, the game gives them a "hand of cards" consisting of a semi-random selection of technologies available for research, which are picked randomly from a hidden "deck of cards" consisting of all valid research options that can appear. A new hand of cards will be drawn whenever a research project is completed, and its technology researched.

Technologies are divided into 6 tiers (T0 to T5) of advancement. Higher tier technologies require obtaining a certain number of technologies from the preceding tier in the same area of research (set at 6 for all tiers) before they become available as research alternatives.

Every time the player meets the requirements for a given technology to become obtainable, the technology in question is added into the main "card deck" and then has a chance of appearing in the "card hand" whenever the game draws a new hand for the player to pick from. There is one basic parameter affecting a tech's chances of appearing in a given card hand:

- Weight – A base value denoting the relative chance (out of all the valid options) of a particular technology to be drawn as an alternative. This may be further modified by an empire's composition (ethics, civics, etc.) and its current state (scientist's traits, past tech, etc.).

To further increase variation, a technology which appeared as an alternative in the previous card hand has its weight halved in the next draw, resetting after that.

In general, the more advanced a technology is, the lower its weight (and the higher its cost). Systematically important techs (e.g. terraforming) have a higher weight (typically between 150% and double normal) to help ensure empires get a chance to research them, whereas rare rare technologies have significantly lower weight (typically one-eighth of the normal without the matching expertise).

Research can be automated, in which case the game picks the cheapest technology available to research unless a rare technology is available for research, in which case the game will pick that. Note that AI players do not operate this way, and instead have a more complex logic for determining what to research.

- Example

Let's assume the game draws a card hand of 3 techs: Armored Torpedoes, Autocannons, and Exotic Gas Refining. Additionally, a councilor scientist has the Expertise: Propulsion 24px Scientist veteran eng 2 Expertise: Propulsion II trait (matching Armored Torpedoes), and the previous card hand had Autocannons as an available option.

\text{Total weight} = \text{Armored Torpedoes weight}\, \cdot\, \text{expertise bonus} +\, \text{Autocannons weight}\, +\, \text{Exotic Gas Refining weight}

\text{Total weight} = 60 \cdot 1.25\, +\, \frac{75}{2}\, +\, 170 = 75 +\, 37.5 +\, 170 = 282.5

If these were the only three valid techs and only one tech were to be drawn, then each tech's chances of being drawn would be 26.5%, 13.3%, and 60.2% respectively (rounded to 1 decimal place). Realistically, there are usually many more valid picks and so the probability of picking any given tech is significantly lower than the figures given here.

- Research alternatives

By default, each card hand drawn contains a selection of 3 researchable technologies, or research alternatives, but this number can be further increased by a variety of factors. Additionally, some research cards may be gained as permanent alternatives. They appear below the regular alternatives and are distinguished from them by a acquire golden border surrounding the tech card's bezel. These alternatives are usually acquired (along with some partial progress) through post-battle debris analysis, from special projects, anomalies, archaeological site, situations, or other events. These options will always appear as available options when drawing a new card hand and will remain as such until fully researched.

If need be, it is possible to change an on-going research project at any point – without losing research progress – and continue researching it at a later time. It is important to note, however, that the research progress is only saved as an absolute value and not a percentage, and therefore does not scale with changes to technology costs (for better or for worse). This means that if a technology is left partially researched and the empire's empire size increases before it is fully researched, this will cause the technology's relative progress percentage to decrease as technology cost increases alongside empire size.

Unless a given technology card has appeared as a permanent alternative, there is no guarantee for said technology card to appear again in the next card hand drawn, although it will reappear again eventually through sheer probability after enough new hands have been drawn, and the more research alternatives that each card hand contains, the higher the probability of it appearing as one of them.

The number of research alternatives per card hand can be increased by the following: Research alternatives

- Research progress

In general, research time can be summarized as the following formula:

\text{Research time} = \sum\frac{\text{Research cost} -\, \text{Partial research done} }{ \text{Monthly research progress} }

Research progress is one of the key elements affecting the time it takes to discover new technologies. It is formulated as follows:

\text{Monthly research progress} = \text{Research resource produced}\, \cdot\, \sum\text{Research speed modifiers}\, +\, \text{min}[\text{Research resource stored},\text{Research resource produced}]

While it is possible for the monthly research progress to remain constant during the course of researching a certain technology, it is more than likely to fluctuate – for better or for worse – due to consequences, effects and outcomes of various actions (such as exploration, empire development, expansion, etc.). This, in turn, may increase or decrease the total research time of a given tech.

The most prominent example of this is empire size. If empire size increases above 100, then every additional point of empire size above that will increase the research cost of technologies by +0,2% per point.

- Example

The empire from the previous examples (same setup) has just finished debris analysis granting it +10% research progress in Armored Torpedoes along with engineering research (stored research).

This setup generates the following monthly research progress:

\text{Monthly research progress} = 24\, \cdot\, (1\, +\, 0.05\, +\, 0.15)\, +\, \text{min}[1000, 24] = 52.8

Assuming no further changes impact the above setup, the total research time of the tech would be:

\text{Research time} = \frac{1862\, -\, 1862 \cdot\, 0.1 }{ 52.8 } = \text{31.74 months}

Note: Partial research can refer to debris analysis, previous research, event rewards, etc.

- Debris

Debris has a chance of spawning when at least one ship from a hostile enemy fleet is destroyed. Debris can provide progress on most components, weapons, and defenses, but not ship upgrades. The following are examples of technologies that cannot be obtained from debris:

- Standardized Corvette Patterns (or any other cost-reducing technologies)
- Improved Corvette Hulls (or any other non-component ship upgrade technologies)
- Destroyers (or any other ship hull size)
- Synapse Interceptors (or any other repeatable technologies)
- Psionic Shields (or any other Psionic technologies)

Each component can only spawn if the components are above the technology level of the empire researching the debris. Each component debris provides 10% progress on the technology, or 10% progress on the prerequisite technology if the prerequisite technology is unresearched. If no component can be spawned, then debris will give a small amount of stored research from a relevant area instead.

If the policy is Scavenge, no research benefit will be gained, and debris will instead yield resources equal to 10% of the ship's build cost.

If the destroyed ships belonged to an empire that has the Enigmatic Engineering ascension perk, then those ships will not leave any debris.

- Salvager trait and Scavengers civic

The Scavengers and Refurbishment Division civics enable the policy Research & Salvage Debris which allows for debris to generate both research and resources as well as a chance to salvage a ship of equal hull size from said debris; without those civics, only Research or Scavenge can be chosen and the ability to salvage ships requires a scientist with the Salvager 24px veteran Scientist Salvager or Master Salvager 24px veteran Scientist Master Salvager traits to be in the same system.

If Research & Salvage Debris is enabled and a scientist with the Salvager or Master Salvager trait is in the same system, there is an additional 5% combo bonus chance to salvage a ship.

The precise formula is as follows; the same chance is applied independently for each potential salvageable ship in the debris:

\% \text{ chance to salvage ships from debris} = (10 + \text{additional salvage chance} + \text{combo bonus}) \cdot \text{Salvager trait level}

The final salvage chance is calculated as the sum of additional bonuses and combo bonuses, namely from the Scavengers civic (which gives +10% additional salvage chance) and its associated Master Scrapper council position (which gives +1% salvage chance per leader level) as well as the the Salvager 24px veteran Scientist Salvager or Master Salvager 24px veteran Scientist Master Salvager traits (which give a +10%/+20%+30% and +15% salvage chance, respectively), multiplied by the Salvager trait level of the salvaging scientist. If none are present, then the respective value is set to 0. The minimum base salvage chance is 10% without civic, council, combo or trait bonuses, but the Scavengers civic doubles this to a minimum of 20%.

If multiple scientists with Salvager traits are present in the same system, then their trait levels will be tallied up additively to calculate the "Salvager trait level" value. If a scientist with Master Salvager is present, they will apply a 1.5 multiplier to the result of that value. Thus, having two level 3 Salvagers and a Master Salvager in the same system would give a "Salvager trait level" value of 9, equating to a 9 times multiplier to the base additive chance as the result.

- Research output

Each research area employs the use of a different research resource.

Each of these individual resources has a base production of 10 research points a month. Most research output comes from pops working the appropriate jobs or research stations on space deposits.

Research production can be modified for total empire production, job output, research stations (and starbase buildings), or for researcher category jobs. Note, governors only provide the full effect of their traits on the planet they directly govern, and half of that to all other planets in the sector. Other modifiers can affect research output by changing base research output or affecting all resources from jobs.

- Stored research

Whenever research output is not actively used, it will accumulate as stored research. Stored research also includes research resources gained from other avenues that give lump sums of research in bulk, such as debris analysis, anomalies, events, etc.

This allows for a more "relaxed" approach to research by eliminating the potential loss of research points due to forgetting to pick a research project while, at the same time, also simulating accelerated periods of research (as opposed to sudden "jumps") caused by newfound knowledge sources. The current storage levels can be seen by hovering over the appropriate resources.

Once a research project is initiated, any accumulated stored research will be consumed at a rate matching the current output, effectively doubling the total research output, until the amount of stored research left falls below the monthly output, after which any remaining stored research will be consumed in the next month to empty the storage. If the monthly research output changes, then the consumption rate will also adjust accordingly.

- Example
An empire produces engineering research each month and has just finished a debris analysis granting it engineering research, which is collected as stored research.

\text{Stored research expenditure length} = \frac{\text{1000}}{ \text{24}} =\, \text{41.67 months}

When researching, the empire will supplement its engineering research by an additional +24 research points for the next 41 months, then supplement it by +16 research points in the 42nd month, after which the stored engineering research is completely depleted.

- Research speed

Research speed represents a given expertise in a particular research area or field leading to shortened research time of related technologies.

Research speed boosts the effective research production in the following manner:

\text{Effective research production} = \text{Research resource produced}\, \cdot\, \sum\text{Research speed modifiers}

The most immediate sources of research speed modifiers are the scientists in your council. As the applied bonus depends on a scientist's skill level and overall traits, it is recommended to assign newly recruited scientists to command a science ship. Scientists on exploration duty tend to gain experience faster and, if one is in luck, they may also gain a new trait beneficial to research while leveling up.

- Example
An empire is a Materialist and produces engineering research a month. It has a councilor scientist with Expertise: Propulsion 24px Scientist veteran eng 3 Expertise: Propulsion III while researching Armored Torpedoes.

\text{Effective research production} = 24\, \cdot\, (1\, +\, 0.05\, +\, 0.15)\, = 28.8

{{Version|4.5}} {{Technav}} ''Technology'' in Stellaris is divided into 3 research areas with each area corresponding with one of the research resources: {{iconify|Engineering}}, {{iconify|Physics}} and {{iconify|Society}}. Additionally, each of the ~400 techs belongs to one of 13 subcategories divided between the areas (most appearing pre-dominantly in one area though not exclusively). The user interaction aspect utilizes a ''card shuffle'' approach rather than a traditional ''tech tree'' presentation, thereby introducing an element of semi-randomness into the system. Each technology has a ''base cost'' which is modified by "Technology and Tradition Cost" (from [[galaxy settings]] set when starting a new game) and by {{iconify|empire size}} (the research cost is increased by {{red|0.2%}} for each point of empire size above 100). == Research areas & fields == {{anchor|Categories}} [[File:UI tech.png|right|thumb|400px|Technology interface. Every slot here can have one research project active at a time and every research area has its own slot.]] There are three different main ''research areas'' in-game, with each area corresponding with one of the research resources. Additionally, each research area has multiple subcategories, for a total of 13 such subcategories, and every tech belongs to one of these subcategories. The areas and their subcategories are as follows: '''{{icon|Physics}} [[Physics research]]''' {{#lst:Physics research|tech fields}} '''{{icon|Society}} [[Society research]]''' {{#lst:Society research|tech fields}} '''{{icon|Engineering}} [[Engineering research]]''' {{#lst:Engineering research|tech fields}} == Technology cards == [[File:Card system.png|thumb|400px|The "card" system. Every time a research project is to be initiated, the game draws a hand of cards like this one from which the player then can pick one technology to research. (Note that these particular cards shown are obsolete and do not exist in-game)]] Although the underlying technology system is based on the familiar ''tech tree'' structure, it does away with the traditional interaction/presentation in favor of the ''card shuffle'' approach. This injects a semi-random element into research, making it somewhat less predictable as well as less linear. Whenever the player is prompted to initiate a research project, the game gives them a "hand of cards" consisting of a semi-random selection of technologies available for research, which are picked randomly from a hidden "deck of cards" consisting of all valid research options that can appear. A new hand of cards will be drawn whenever a research project is completed, and its technology researched. Technologies are divided into 6 tiers (T0 to T5) of advancement. Higher tier technologies require obtaining a certain number of technologies from the preceding tier in the same area of research (set at 6 for all tiersSee {{path|common/technology/tier/00_tier.txt}} for details.) before they become available as research alternatives. Every time the player meets the requirements for a given technology to become obtainable, the technology in question is added into the main "card deck" and then has a chance of appearing in the "card hand" whenever the game draws a new hand for the player to pick from. There is one basic parameter affecting a tech's chances of appearing in a given card hand: * ''Weight'' – A base value denoting the ''relative'' chance (out of all the valid options) of a particular technology to be drawn as an alternative. This may be further modified by an empire's composition (ethics, civics, etc.) and its current state (scientist's traits, past tech, etc.). To further increase variation, a technology which appeared as an alternative in the previous card hand has its weight halved in the next draw, resetting after that. In general, the more advanced a technology is, the lower its weight (and the higher its cost). Systematically important techs (e.g. terraforming) have a higher weight (typically between 150% and double normal) to help ensure empires get a chance to research them, whereas {{tech color|rare|rare technologies}} have significantly lower weight (typically one-eighth of the normal without the matching expertise). Note that [[AI players]] '''do not''' operate this way, and instead have a more complex logic for determining what to research. === Example === Let's assume the game draws a card hand of 3 techs: {{iconify|Armored Torpedoes|24px|suf=tech}}, {{iconify|Autocannons|24px|suf=tech}}, and {{iconify|Exotic Gas Refining|24px}}. Additionally, a councilor scientist has the {{trait|Expertise: Propulsion|w=24px|class=Scientist|rarity=veteran|bg=eng|tier=2}} Expertise: Propulsion II trait (matching Armored Torpedoes), and the previous card hand had {{iconify|Autocannons|24px|suf=tech}} as an available option. \text{Total weight} = \text{Armored Torpedoes weight}\, \cdot\, \text{expertise bonus} +\, \text{Autocannons weight}\, +\, \text{Exotic Gas Refining weight} \text{Total weight} = 60 \cdot 1.25\, +\, \frac{75}{2}\, +\, 170 = 75 +\, 37.5 +\, 170 = 282.5 If these were the only three valid techs and only one tech were to be drawn, then each tech's chances of being drawn would be '''26.5%''', '''13.3%''', and '''60.2%''' respectively (rounded to 1 decimal place). Realistically, there are usually many more valid picks and so the probability of picking any given tech is significantly lower than the figures given here. === Research alternatives === By default, each card hand drawn contains a selection of 3 researchable technologies, or ''research'' ''alternatives'', but this number can be further increased by a variety of factors. Additionally, some research cards may be gained as ''permanent alternatives''. They appear below the regular alternatives and are distinguished from them by a {{tech color|acquire|golden}} border surrounding the tech card's bezel. These alternatives are usually acquired (along with some partial progress) through [[#debris|post-battle debris analysis]], from [[special projects]], [[anomaly|anomalies]], [[archaeological site]], [[situations]], or other [[events]]. These options will always appear as available options when drawing a new card hand and will remain as such until fully researched. If need be, it is possible to change an on-going research project at any point – without losing research progress – and continue researching it at a later time. It is important to note, however, that the research progress is only saved as an absolute value and not a percentage, and therefore does '''not''' scale with changes to technology costs (for better or for worse). This means that if a technology is left partially researched and the empire's {{iconify|empire size}} increases before it is fully researched, this will cause the technology's relative progress percentage to decrease as technology cost increases alongside empire size. Unless a given technology card has appeared as a permanent alternative, there is no guarantee for said technology card to appear again in the next card hand drawn, although it will reappear again eventually through sheer probability after enough new hands have been drawn, and the more research alternatives that each card hand contains, the higher the probability of it appearing as one of them. The number of research alternatives per card hand can be increased by the following: {{#lsth:Stat modifiers|Research alternatives}} == Research progress == In general, ''research time'' can be summarized as the following formula: \text{Research time} = \sum\frac{\text{Research cost} -\, \text{Partial research done} }{ \text{Monthly research progress} } Research progress is one of the key elements affecting the time it takes to discover new technologies. It is formulated as follows: \text{Monthly research progress} = \text{Research resource produced}\, \cdot\, \sum\text{Research speed modifiers}\, +\, \text{min}[\text{Research resource stored},\text{Research resource produced}] While it is possible for the ''monthly research progress'' to remain constant during the course of researching a certain technology, it is more than likely to fluctuate – for better or for worse – due to consequences, effects and outcomes of various actions (such as exploration, empire development, expansion, etc.). This, in turn, may increase or decrease the total research time of a given tech. The most prominent example of this is {{iconify|empire size}}. If empire size increases above '''100''', then every additional point of empire size above that will increase the research cost of technologies by {{Red|+0,2%}} per point. === Example === The empire from the previous examples (same setup) has just finished debris analysis granting it {{green|+10%}} research progress in {{iconify|Armored Torpedoes|24px|suf=tech}} along with {{iconify|engineering||+1000|green}} research (stored research). This setup generates the following monthly research progress: \text{Monthly research progress} = 24\, \cdot\, (1\, +\, 0.05\, +\, 0.15)\, +\, \text{min}[1000, 24] = 52.8 Assuming no further changes impact the above setup, the total research time of the tech would be: \text{Research time} = \frac{1862\, -\, 1862 \cdot\, 0.1 }{ 52.8 } = \text{31.74 months} '''Note:''' ''Partial research'' can refer to debris analysis, previous research, event rewards, etc. == Debris == Debris has a chance of spawning when at least one ship from a hostile enemy fleet is destroyed. Debris can provide progress on most components, weapons, and defenses, but not ship upgrades. The following are examples of technologies that '''cannot''' be obtained from debris: * {{iconify|Standardized Corvette Patterns|24px}} (or any other cost-reducing technologies) * {{iconify|Improved Corvette Hulls|24px}} (or any other non-[[Ship designer|component]] ship upgrade technologies) * {{iconify|Destroyers|24px|suf=tech}} (or any other ship hull size) * {{iconify|Synapse Interceptors|24px|tech=repeat}} (or any other repeatable technologies) * {{iconify|Psionic Shields|24px|suf=tech|tech=acquire}} (or any other Psionic technologies) Each component can only spawn if the components are above the technology level of the empire researching the debris. Each component debris provides {{green|10%}} progress on the technology, or {{green|10%}} progress on the prerequisite technology if the prerequisite technology is unresearched. If no component can be spawned, then debris will give a small amount of stored research from a relevant area instead. If the {{iconify|policy||debris}} is ''Scavenge'', no research benefit will be gained, and debris will instead yield [[resources]] equal to 10% of the ship's build cost. If the destroyed ships belonged to an empire that has the {{iconify|Enigmatic Engineering}} ascension perk, then those ships will not leave any debris. === Salvager trait and Scavengers civic === The {{iconify|Scavengers}} and {{iconify|Refurbishment Division}} civics enable the {{iconify|policy||debris}} ''Research & Salvage Debris'' which allows for debris to generate both research and resources as well as a chance to salvage a ship of equal hull size from said debris; without those civics, only ''Research'' or ''Scavenge'' can be chosen and the ability to salvage ships requires a {{iconify|scientist}} with the {{trait|Salvager|w=24px|rarity=veteran|class=Scientist}} Salvager or {{trait|Master Salvager|w=24px|rarity=veteran|class=Scientist}} Master Salvager traits to be in the same system. If ''Research & Salvage Debris'' is enabled and a scientist with the Salvager or Master Salvager trait is in the same system, there is an additional 5% combo bonus chance to salvage a ship. The precise formula is as follows; the same chance is applied independently for each potential salvageable ship in the debris: \% \text{ chance to salvage ships from debris} = (10 + \text{additional salvage chance} + \text{combo bonus}) \cdot \text{Salvager trait level}See {{path|common/script_values/01_script_values_paragons.txt country_salvage_ships_from_debris_chance}} for formula details The final salvage chance is calculated as the sum of additional bonuses and combo bonuses, namely from the Scavengers civic (which gives {{Green|+10%}} additional salvage chance) and its associated Master Scrapper [[council]] position (which gives {{Green|+1%}} salvage chance per leader level) as well as the the {{trait|Salvager|w=24px|rarity=veteran|class=Scientist}} Salvager or {{trait|Master Salvager|w=24px|rarity=veteran|class=Scientist}} Master Salvager traits (which give a {{Green|+10%}}/{{Green|+20%}}{{Green|+30%}} and {{Green|+15%}} salvage chance, respectively), multiplied by the Salvager trait level of the salvaging scientist. If none are present, then the respective value is set to 0. The minimum base salvage chance is '''10%''' without civic, council, combo or trait bonuses, but the Scavengers civic doubles this to a minimum of '''20%'''. If multiple scientists with Salvager traits are present in the same system, then their trait levels will be tallied up additively to calculate the "Salvager trait level" value. If a scientist with Master Salvager is present, they will apply a 1.5 multiplier to the result of that value. Thus, having two level 3 Salvagers and a Master Salvager in the same system would give a "Salvager trait level" value of 9, equating to a 9 times multiplier to the base additive chance as the result. accumulate as ''stored research''. Stored research also includes research resources gained from other avenues that give lump sums of research in bulk, such as debris analysis, anomalies, events, etc. This allows for a more "relaxed" approach to research by eliminating the potential loss of research points due to forgetting to pick a research project while, at the same time, also simulating accelerated periods of research (as opposed to sudden "jumps") caused by newfound knowledge sources. The current storage levels can be seen by hovering over the appropriate resources. Once a research project is initiated, any accumulated stored research will be consumed at a rate matching the current output, effectively doubling the total research output, until the amount of stored research left falls below the monthly output, after which any remaining stored research will be consumed in the next month to empty the storage. If the monthly research output changes, then the consumption rate will also adjust accordingly. ; Example An empire produces {{iconify|engineering||+24|green}} research each month and has just finished a debris analysis granting it {{iconify|engineering||+1000|green}} research, which is collected as stored research. \text{Stored research expenditure length} = \frac{\text{1000}}{ \text{24}} =\, \text{41.67 months} When researching, the empire will supplement its {{iconify|engineering}} research by an additional {{green|+24}} research points for the next 41 months, then supplement it by {{green|+16}} research points in the 42nd month, after which the stored {{iconify|engineering}} research is completely depleted. == Research speed == ''Research speed'' represents a given expertise in a particular research area or field leading to shortened research time of related technologies. Research speed boosts the effective research production in the following manner: \text{Effective research production} = \text{Research resource produced}\, \cdot\, \sum\text{Research speed modifiers} The most immediate sources of research speed modifiers are the [[scientists]] in your council. As the applied bonus depends on a scientist's skill level and overall traits, it is recommended to assign newly recruited scientists to command a [[science ship]]. Scientists on exploration duty tend to gain experience faster and, if one is in luck, they may also gain a new trait beneficial to research while leveling up. ; Example An empire is a {{iconify|Materialist}} and produces {{iconify|engineering||+24|green}} research a month. It has a councilor scientist with {{trait|Expertise: Propulsion|w=24px|class=Scientist|rarity=veteran|bg=eng|tier=3}} Expertise: Propulsion III while researching {{iconify|Armored Torpedoes|24px|suf=tech}}. \text{Effective research production} = 24\, \cdot\, (1\, +\, 0.05\, +\, 0.15)\, = 28.8 '''Note:''' An empire without a {{iconify|Head of Research}} councilor receives a {{red|−25%}} penalty to research speed. In Stellaris, the economy is based on production and consumption of resources and services, either from a specific planet or throughout the empire. It relies primarily on pops working jobs to produce most resources, with mining or research stations built over space deposits as a secondary source. Certain buildings and other sources can produce resources as well.

Resources can vary from fairly common food crops to very rare substances such as dark matter and also abstract concepts such as influence and research.

There are two kinds of resources: Material and Abstract. In addition, certain empire capacities (e.g. naval capacity) or planetary values (e.g. amenities) are "produced" in a similar way to resources. If an empire's stored stockpile for a material resource drops to 0 with negative income, for most material resources it triggers a Shortage situation and for rare and abstract resources, it gives an empire-wide penalty.

- Resource storage capacity

All resources can be stockpiled. All empires have a 15,000 starting storage capacity for each material resource except trade, which has a 50,000 starting storage capacity. An empire can build resource silo Resource Silos 30 Resource Silos buildings on colonies and Resource Silo buildings on starbases to expand their storage capacity. In addition, when the Galactic Market is founded, all members of the Galactic Community gain 10,000 storage capacity unless the the greater good Universal Prosperity Mandate resolution has been passed, and researching Mega-Engineering adds 20,000 to an empire's storage capacity. When an empire's storage capacity for a resource is reached, any additional production of that resource is simply lost.

For abstract resources, only influence has a maximum storage capacity: 1,000. Unity and research have unlimited storage capacity; stored research is automatically used when researching a technology or special project, for more see stored research.

- Material resources

Material resources are the primary means of developing an empire's infrastructure. Most construction – whether buildings, districts, ships, or other – requires at least one material resource. Additionally, material resources are used for most upkeep, from pops to ships to megastructures and more.

Resource deposits the empire does not have the technology to exploit will appear greyed out on map.

- Basic resources

Basic resources are directly gathered from orbital deposits or by jobs from resource districts. Biomass is only available to empires with the Wilderness origin.
Resource | Description
Energy credits | energy Energy Credits are stored units of transferrable energy that are essential for all space-faring empires. They are used for upkeep of Ships and Buildings, to clear planetary tile blocker Blockers, and when making deals with others. Food | food Food represents the various nutrients required to sustain and grow Pops. To increase: - Build district Agriculture Districts - Buy on the market fee Market Driven Assimilators produce food Food for their pop Cyborg Pops, and Rogue Servitors for their pop Bio-Trophy Pops. Machine Intelligences and Thermophiles generally do not use this resource.
Trade | trade value Trade represents the everyday economic activity, flow of commerce, and logistics capacity within an empire. It is used for Ship Upkeep, Colony Upkeep, and to buy other resources. To increase: - Construct Buildings with Jobs that produce trade Trade - Build Mining Stations on interstellar trade deposits - Sell resources on the market fee Market

There is still income and upkeep of minerals Minerals and energy Energy Credits, but managed as a Situation. One point of Operational Reserves is equal to one minerals Mineral or one energy Energy Credit. One point of Operational Reserve Capacity has a base value of 15000. Each Arkship we own increases it by: Tier I: 5000 Tier II: 7500 Tier III: 10000 Civilian Arkships grant an additional per 2500 Tier. The Stages of the situation affect the empire's Arkships in different ways, and Approaches can be selected to conserve resources or burn through them for higher productivity. Minerals and Energy Credits can be bought on the market fee Market, but not sold.

- Advanced resources

Advanced resources are produced by jobs which refine them from minerals. Gestalt Consciousness empires do not use or produce consumer goods unless they have the Rogue Servitor or Obsessional Directive civic or are paying some monthly expense of the resource (for instance paying contribution to a subject or overlord).

Resource | Description

To increase: - Build Mixed Industry or Heavy Industry - Build building Alloy Foundries - Buy on the market fee Market

Machine Intelligences with an Obsessional Directive produce consumer goods Consumer Goods, as do Rogue Servitors for their pop Bio-Trophy Pops. Hive Minds do not use this resource. Machine Intelligences generally do not use this resource.

- Strategic resources

Strategic resources are specialized resources required to both build and maintain advanced buildings and ship components. They are harder to obtain than the common basic and advanced resources and are therefore also much more highly valued. Strategic resources can be obtained by either extracting them from natural space or planetary deposits or manufacturing them synthetically. Natural strategic resource deposits are always visible but requires specific technologies to exploit. Synthetic versions are produced from minerals, albeit at a steep price. All strategic resources can also be manufactured from Fallen Empires' Dimensional Fabricator buildings.

- Abstract resources

Abstract resources represent an empire's sociopolitical and technological capabilities.

It is used for strategic actions, for example to build Outposts, make Claims, and maintain Diplomatic Pacts. Generation of Influence remains fairly stable, but it can be improved. - Empire caps

Empire caps impose various limits on the expansion of an empire.
Resource | Description
Envoy | Envoys handle First Contact with unknown aliens, manage spy networks, and engage in Diplomacy with other Empires. To increase: - Build an Interstellar Assembly Megastructure - Utilize certain Buildings, Leader Traits, and Civics - Unlock the Federation perk Federal Envoys
Station Capacity | Station Capacity shows the number of upgraded Starbases and Waystation that can be effectively supported, not counting Outposts. Exceeding Station Capacity increases Station Upkeep. To increase: - Acquire more Owned Systems - Utilize certain technologies and traditions
Naval Capacity | Naval Capacity shows the combined Fleet Size that can be effectively supported. Exceeding Naval Capacity increases Ship Upkeep. To increase: - Build Anchorage modules on Starbases - Utilize certain Jobs, for example from a building Stronghold - Utilize certain technologies and traditions

- The market

The market is available to every empire from the start, and represents various actors within an empire with whom the empire itself can buy and sell resources. Resources are bought and sold for Trade, with their prices dependent on empire economy, supply and demand, and whether the galactic market is founded. The price can go as low as 20% and as high as 500% of the base price, further subject to market fee. Resources can be purchased or sold either in bulk (bottom left of the Market screen) or by setting up an automatic monthly trade order (bottom right, see below).

If too much of a resource is bought in a single month, the price for that resource will rise for the following month(s); if too much is sold, the price will drop. This is true for both bulk purchases (left side of screen) and automated Monthly Trades (right side), and the two are additive for any given month. Returning any buying/selling of that resource to within the values listed will, over time, shift the price back toward and eventually to the Base Price.

The market base prices are the following:
Resource | trade Base price | Maximum automatic trade to keep internal market values at base price
Buy | Sell
energymineralsfood | 1 | 42 | 64
consumer goods | 2 | 21 | 32
alloys | 4 | 10 | 16
exotic gasesrare crystalsvolatile motes | 10 | 4 | 6
dark matterliving metalzro | 20 | 2 | 3

- Automated trading

In the right lower area of the Market screen, a player can "Add new monthly trade", to automatically buy or sell a specified amount of any or all of the 5 basic resources (energy Energy Credits, minerals Minerals, food Food, consumer goods Consumer Goods, and/or alloys Alloys) each month. Optionally, the player can also, in the same area, specify a maximum or minimum price, which is useful if the player wishes to return the current price back to the Base Price (see table and comments, previous).

When selecting an amount to Buy, it's important to understand that all purchases are paid for with stored Trade; if you don't have enough Trade stored, you cannot make the Purchase. This amount does not include "future" Trade, only what you currently have on hand.

Similarly, when selecting an amount to Sell, it's also important to understand that the Market does not allow the player to sell "future" production, i.e. you can only sell what you have currently stored before the date clicks over from the 30th to the 1st of the next month. You cannot sell based on your monthly "income", only what is currently listed as "stored".

Lastly, and of equal importance, understand that, if a Sale order is more than is available, that sale will not be made! The game will not sell "what is available" and partially complete the order, it will simply ignore the excessive sale order entirely and sell zero that turn.* With this in mind, be aware that +/- resource production values included in the top margin are rounded nearest - mouse-hover over the value to make sure you are not selling a fraction over the monthly income.
- (* Note: At the time of this posting (July 2025), it is not known if this is working as intended or not, it is simply the observed current mechanic.)

- Example:
- A player wants to build a Colony Ship, which will cost 200 Food, 200 Consumer Goods, and 200 Alloys. They currently have 225 Food stored, and a surplus Food production of +35, so while waiting to get enough of CG's and Alloys, they are selling off their extra Food, -35/Turn, so the 225 stored Food value stays stable. The player has carefully balanced the rest of their Purchase and Sales around that, so their Trade is also stable.

- They finally get 200(+) of both Consumer Goods and Alloys, and Build their Colony Ship. {225 Food -200} leaves them with 25 Food stored. They do not adjust their standing automated Food Sell order, so it remains at -35/month.
- Next turn, there is not enough food stored to cover the -35 monthly Sell order, so that is ignored, and 0 Food is sold and +0 Trade is generated from Food sales this month. The full value of 35 Food production is applied, leaving the player with 60 food stored (previous 25 + 35 production), and a drop in Trade income from the loss of 35 Food sold.

- The turn after that, there is then enough Food (60) to cover the -35 Sell order, so that monthly Sell order is completed successfully, leaving 60 Food stored (60 stored previously, -35 sold, +35 produced), and the Trade income returns as it was previously.

- Galactic market

The galactic market is created via the Form the Galactic Market galactic focus in the Galactic Community. Once the focus is set the Galactic Market Nomination will begin. For 5 years, eligible empires may boost their chances of being selected as the market nexus by nominating one of their planets and further by boosting their nomination bid.

The host for the galactic market is chosen through two random rolls. The first happens when the Galactic Market Hub Nomination decision is enacted on a planet. This randomly assigns a rating ranging from Weak to Strong to the planet according to the weightings listed below, under Nomination rating chance. Improving the trade output the planet later on will not improve the rating of the planet, however the nomination can be revoked and then repaid to reroll the weighting. Additionally, this rating can be improved to the next higher rating by passing the Boost Nomination Bid decision up to two times. Each empire can only nominate a single planet.

Once 5 years have passed, the second random roll happens, determining the planet to host the galactic market. In this roll, each planet is weighted according to the rating of the owning empire's nominated planet, if any, and the total trade value produced in the system, using this calculation:

- Start with the empire's market nomination rating as a number from 1 (None) to 6 (Perfect).
- Multiply by the total trade value produced in the same system as the planet. This includes the planet itself, all other colonies in the same system, and any trade value deposits in the same system. It does not include trade gathered from other systems by the starbase.
- If the specific planet is not nominated, divide by 10.
- Raise to the exponent of 1.5.

For example, a planet with a Strong nomination that produces 90 trade value, with another planet in the system that produces 10 trade value, would have a winning weight of (4 * 100)1.5 = 8000. The other planet in the same system would have a winning weight of (4 * 100 / 10)1.5 = 252.98. A planet in another system with 10 trade value, owned by the same empire, would have a winning weight of (4 * 10 / 10)1.5 = 8.

Winning weight is effectively the chance of each planet succeeding in the bid. Your chance of winning is calculated using {Your Winning Weight \over All Winning Weights}

The lottery weights are:
Rating | Nomination rating chance | Winning weight multiplier | Requirements (any of)
None | – | x1 | No nomination, all eligible empires
Weak - 9 - ×2 if trade value below 50 - ×0.5 if trade value above 80 - ×0.5 if trade value above 120 - ×0.33 if Corporate authority - ×1.5 if Gestalt Consciousness | x2 | Planet nominated
Adequate | 6 | x3 | Planet nominated Weak rating and boosted once
Strong - 1 - ×0.5 if trade value below 50 - ×1.5 if trade value above 80 - ×2 if trade value above 120 - x9 if Corporate authority - x0.75 if Gestalt Consciousness - x200 if planet is Ecumenopolis | x4 | Planet nominated Adequate rating and boosted once Weak rating and boosted twice
Exceptional | – | x5 | Strong rating and boosted once Adequate rating and boosted twice
Perfect | – | x6 | Strong rating and boosted twice

Empires may only access and trade on the galactic market if they are a member of the Galactic Community. The owner of the galactic market system enjoys a reduction in its market fee. Supply and demand on the galactic market affects the prices for every empire, and large shifts in prices will affect the economy of every empire relying on importing or exporting a resource. Resources will only become available after at least one empire has them in storage.

If the empire hosting the galactic market leaves the galactic community the nomination process will start again to choose a new host. If the hosting empire loses ownership of the system with the galactic market, the market system will be relocated if that system has no owner or is now held by an empire who is not a member of the galactic community, with the galactic market station relocating to a weighted random galactic community member's capital system.

- Slave market

mgc
Access to the slave market is granted once the galactic market is founded. Only empires that also have access to the galactic market will be able to use the slave market. Only pops that are enslaved are able to be sold on the slave market, with a base price of 1000 Trade, raised or lowered by species traits. Mechanical pops can be bought and sold on the market if enslaved or non-sentient. Empires will be notified if there are slaves of their founder species put on sale.

Empires that have the slavery policy set to Outlawed will set free any pop bought on the slave market, but the pop price will be doubled.

fed
The slave market can be closed first for organic species and then for all species via Galactic Community resolutions.

- Market fee

All sales or purchases on the internal and galactic market have a market fee added to them. The market fee starts at 30% and cannot go below 5%. It can be altered by the following:
- Trader Proxy Office starbase buildings: −5% each
- mercantile Insider Trading iconify tradition: −10%
- versatility Adaptive Programming iconify tradition: −10%
- cosSecrets of the Inetian Traders: -5%
- Galactic Stock Exchange: -5% (only once per empire)
- Corporate Dominion Trader Liaison: -1% (per skill level)
- Hosting the Galactic Market: −10%
- The Economic Sanctions Galactic Community resolution will increase the market fee by +10% per level of the sanctions (max +30%).

''To increase:'' # Build {{yellow|Anchorage}} modules on Starbases # Utilize certain {{iconify|Job}}s, for example from a {{icon|building}} Stronghold # Utilize certain technologies and traditions |} == The market == [[File:UI Market.png|320px|thumb|The market]] The market is available to every empire from the start, and represents various actors within an empire with whom the empire itself can buy and sell resources. Resources are bought and sold for {{iconify|Trade}}, with their prices dependent on empire economy, supply and demand, and whether the galactic market is founded. The price can go as low as 20% and as high as 500% of the base price, further subject to market fee. Resources can be purchased or sold either in bulk (bottom left of the Market screen) or by setting up an automatic monthly trade order (bottom right, [[Resources#Automated trading|see below]]). If too much of a resource is bought in a single month, the price for that resource will rise for the following month(s); if too much is sold, the price will drop. This is true for both bulk purchases (left side of screen) and automated Monthly Trades (right side), and the two are additive for any given month. Returning any buying/selling of that resource to within the values listed will, over time, shift the price back toward and eventually to the Base Price. The market base prices are the following: {| class ="mildtable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! rowspan=2 | Resource !! rowspan=2 | {{icon|trade}} Base price !! colspan=2 | Maximum automatic trade to keep
internal market values at base price |- !         Buy !!         Sell |- | {{icon|energy}}{{icon|minerals}}{{icon|food}} || 1 || 42 || 64 |- | {{icon|consumer goods}} || 2 || 21 || 32 |- | {{icon|alloys}} || 4 || 10 || 16 |- | {{icon|exotic gases}}{{icon|rare crystals}}{{icon|volatile motes}} || 10 || 4 || 6 |- | {{icon|dark matter}}{{icon|living metal}}{{icon|zro}} || 20 || 2 || 3 |} === Automated trading === In the right lower area of the Market screen, a player can "Add new monthly trade", to automatically buy or sell a specified amount of any or all of the 5 basic resources ({{icon|energy}} Energy Credits, {{icon|minerals}} Minerals, {{icon|food}} Food, {{icon|consumer goods}} Consumer Goods, and/or {{icon|alloys}} Alloys) each month. Optionally, the player can also, in the same area, specify a maximum or minimum price, which is useful if the player wishes to return the current price back to the Base Price (see table and comments, previous). When selecting an amount to Buy, it's important to understand that all purchases are paid for with stored {{iconify|Trade}}; if you don't have enough Trade stored, you cannot make the Purchase. This amount does ''not'' include "future" Trade, only what you currently have on hand. Similarly, when selecting an amount to Sell, it's also important to understand that the Market does not allow the player to sell "future" production, i.e. you can only sell what you have ''currently'' stored before the date clicks over from the 30th to the 1st of the next month. You cannot sell based on your monthly "income", only what is currently listed as "stored". Lastly, and of equal importance, understand that, if a Sale order is more than is available, ''that sale will '''not''' be made!'' The game will not sell "what is available" and ''partially'' complete the order, it will simply ignore the excessive sale order entirely and sell zero that turn.* With this in mind, be aware that +/- resource production values included in the top margin are ''rounded nearest'' - mouse-hover over the value to make sure you are not selling a fraction over the monthly income. :: (* Note: At the time of this posting (July 2025), it is not known if this is working as intended or not, it is simply the observed current mechanic.) : Example: :: A player wants to build a Colony Ship, which will cost 200 Food, 200 Consumer Goods, and 200 Alloys. They currently have 225 Food stored, and a surplus Food production of +35, so while waiting to get enough of CG's and Alloys, they are selling off their extra Food, -35/Turn, so the 225 stored Food value stays stable. The player has carefully balanced the rest of their Purchase and Sales around that, so their Trade is also stable. :: They finally get 200(+) of both Consumer Goods and Alloys, and Build their Colony Ship. {225 Food -200} leaves them with 25 Food stored. They do not adjust their standing automated Food Sell order, so it remains at -35/month. :: Next turn, there is not enough food stored to cover the -35 monthly Sell order, so that is ignored, and 0 Food is sold and +0 Trade is generated from Food sales this month. The full value of 35 Food production is applied, leaving the player with 60 food stored (previous 25 + 35 production), and a drop in Trade income from the loss of 35 Food sold. :: The turn after that, there ''is'' then enough Food (60) to cover the -35 Sell order, so that monthly Sell order is completed successfully, leaving 60 Food stored ''(60 stored previously, -35 sold, +35 produced)'', and the Trade income returns as it was previously. === Galactic market === The galactic market is created via the [[File:Galactic focus galactic market.png|24px]] Form the Galactic Market galactic focus in the Galactic Community. Once the focus is set the Galactic Market Nomination will begin. For 5 years, eligible empires may boost their chances of being selected as the market nexus by nominating one of their planets and further by boosting their nomination bid. The host for the galactic market is chosen through two random rolls. The first happens when the [[File:Decision default.png|24px]] Galactic Market Hub Nomination decision is enacted on a planet. This randomly assigns a rating ranging from {{red|Weak}} to {{green|Strong}} to the planet according to the weightings listed below, under ''Nomination rating chance''. Improving the trade output the planet later on will not improve the rating of the planet, however the nomination can be revoked and then repaid to reroll the weighting. Additionally, this rating can be improved to the next higher rating by passing the [[File:Decision default.png|24px]] Boost Nomination Bid decision up to two times. Each empire can only nominate a single planet. Once 5 years have passed, the second random roll happens, determining the planet to host the galactic market. In this roll, each planet is weighted according to the rating of the owning empire's nominated planet, if any, and the total trade value produced in the system, using this calculation: # Start with the empire's market nomination rating as a number from 1 (None) to 6 (Perfect). # Multiply by the total trade value produced in the same system as the planet. This includes the planet itself, all other colonies in the same system, and any trade value deposits in the same system. It does not include trade gathered from other systems by the starbase. # If the specific planet is not nominated, divide by 10. # Raise to the exponent of 1.5. For example, a planet with a Strong nomination that produces 90 trade value, with another planet in the system that produces 10 trade value, would have a winning weight of (4 * 100)1.5 = 8000. The other planet in the same system would have a winning weight of (4 * 100 / 10)1.5 = 252.98. A planet in another system with 10 trade value, owned by the same empire, would have a winning weight of (4 * 10 / 10)1.5 = 8. Winning weight is effectively the chance of each planet succeeding in the bid. Your chance of winning is calculated using {Your Winning Weight \over All Winning Weights} The lottery weights are: {| class ="mildtable plainlist" |- ! Rating !! Nomination rating chance !! Winning weight multiplier !! Requirements (any of) |- | {{red|None}} || – || x1 || No nomination, all eligible empires |- | {{red|Weak}} | * 9 * ×2 if {{iconify|trade value}} below 50 * ×0.5 if {{iconify|trade value}} above 80 * ×0.5 if {{iconify|trade value}} above 120 * ×0.33 if {{iconify|Corporate}} authority * ×1.5 if {{iconify|Gestalt Consciousness}} | x2 || Planet nominated |- | {{yellow|Adequate}} | 6 | x3 || Planet nominated

{{yellow|Adequate}} rating and boosted once

{{yellow|Adequate}} rating and boosted twice |- | {{green|Perfect}} || – || x6 ||{{green|Strong}} rating and boosted twice |} Empires may only access and trade on the galactic market if they are a member of the {{iconify|Galactic Community}}. The owner of the galactic market system enjoys a reduction in its market fee. Supply and demand on the galactic market affects the prices for every empire, and large shifts in prices will affect the economy of every empire relying on importing or exporting a resource. Resources will only become available after at least one empire has them in storage. If the empire hosting the galactic market leaves the galactic community the nomination process will start again to choose a new host. If the hosting empire loses ownership of the system with the galactic market, the market system will be relocated if that system has no owner or is now held by an empire who is not a member of the galactic community, with the galactic market station relocating to a weighted random galactic community member's capital system. ==== Slave market ==== {{expansion|mgc}} Access to the slave market is granted once the galactic market is founded. Only empires that also have access to the galactic market will be able to use the slave market. Only pops that are enslaved are able to be sold on the slave market, with a base price of 1000 {{iconify|Trade}}, raised or lowered by species traits. {{iconify|Mechanical}} pops can be bought and sold on the market if enslaved or non-sentient. Empires will be notified if there are slaves of their founder species put on sale. Empires that have the slavery policy set to ''Outlawed'' will set free any pop bought on the slave market, but the pop price will be doubled. {{expansion|fed}} The slave market can be closed first for organic species and then for all species via Galactic Community resolutions. === Market fee === All sales or purchases on the internal and galactic market have a market fee added to them. The market fee starts at '''30%''' and cannot go below {{green|5%}}. It can be altered by the following: * [[File:Sb offworld trading company.png|24px|link=Starbase#Trader Proxy Office|Trader Proxy Office]] Trader Proxy Office starbase buildings: {{green|−5%}} each * {{tradition|mercantile|Insider Trading|iconify}} tradition: {{green|−10%}} * {{tradition|versatility|Adaptive Programming|iconify}} tradition: {{green|−10%}} * {{icon|cos}}[[Minor_artifacts#Secrets_of_the_Precursors%7CSecrets|Secrets of the Inetian Traders]]: {{green|-5%}} * {{iconify|Galactic Stock Exchange|24px}}: {{green|-5%}} {{small|(only once per empire)}} * {{icon|Corporate Dominion}} [[Council#Enclave_positions|Trader Liaison]]: {{green|-1%}} {{small|(per skill level)}} * Hosting the Galactic Market: {{green|−10%}} * The ''Economic Sanctions'' Galactic Community resolution will increase the market fee by {{red|+10%}} per level of the sanctions (max {{red|+30%}}). == References == {{Template:ConceptsNavbox}} [[Category:Economy]]

building Buildings are structures that can be constructed on a colony, filling the colony's buildings slots. 6 building slots are available on each colony's primary district, and additional building slots are unlocked by district specializations. Buildings may be ruined by orbital bombardment or collateral damage. Buildings that are ruined can be repaired for half of their cost and construction time.

- Building sets

Each building belongs to one or more building sets. A building can only be built in a district that permits one of its building sets and does not exclude any of them, which depends on its specialization. Changing the specialization of a district may change what buildings are supported and the new specialization's tooltip will display which existing buildings will be retained and which ones will be removed.
- The five general building slots available on all planets, as well as the Urban Expansion specialization, can accept most building sets. The main exceptions are extraction buildings, which can only be built in relevant extraction districts.
- Most specializations can accept an automation building, which produces extra workforce. There are several types with different building sets, each of which has a planet limit of 1. They affect all jobs of types created by the district and its buildings, even if created by other districts or their buildings.
- The Civilian Industry specialization can accept buildings relevant to production of consumer goods, as well as rare resource refineries. Similarly the Heavy Industry specialization can accept buildings relevant to production of alloys. Mixed Industry can accept both.
- Research specializations can accept research buildings relevant to their specialization (all of them if it is a generic Research Enclave). Archives can accept both research and unity buildings, whereas Administrative Hubs can only accept unity buildings.
- Resource districts can accept relevant resource buildings, including output boosters such as the Energy Grid. Notably, Bio-Reactors are considered agriculture buildings, since they alter Farmer jobs to produce energy. Some specializations can accept others, for example Mineral Research Support (mining district specialization) can also accept an Applied Mechanics Institute.
- Agrarian Idyll empires can build Agrarian Villages specializations which can accept any "urban" buildings, including energy and mineral extraction.

A total of 21 buildings may be built on a colony. By default the primary district specialization always contains six building slots. Resource districts allow an additional three building slots per specialization.

- Capital buildings

Intro

- Unique buildings

Unique buildings are buildings that can only be built a limited number of times per planet or empire, and typically provide effects beyond the creation of jobs. Many of them require the capital to have reached a certain level.

- Housing buildings

Housing buildings come in two levels and increase Housing and Amenities. They are converted if the world is conquered by an empire that uses a different building line.

- Fallen empire buildings

Fallen empire buildings are the most efficient buildings in the game. Each one takes 600 days to build or upgrade. They are not converted if the world is conquered by an empire lacking the technology to build them and can also be repaired if ruined.

There are four ways an empire can get access to fallen empire building technologies:
- apc If Apocalypse is enabled, empires with the Enigmatic Engineering ascension perk can draw the technologies as research options. (Up to 4 total researched.)
- anr If Ancient Relics is enabled, using the Reverse-Engineer Arcane Technology artifact action has a 20% chance (40% with the Archaeo-Engineers ascension perk) to grant the ability to build a random fallen empire building once.
- tma If The Machine Age is enabled, empires with the Cosmogenesis ascension perk that have reached the required ambition level can draw the technologies as research options.
- bio If BioGenesis is enabled, one of the tasks assigned by the Shattered Fragment fallen empires can have a random fallen empire technology as a reward.
Empires with the Cosmogenesis ascension perk that accepted the Keepers of Knowledge demand to end the crisis path will no longer be able to build fallen empire buildings, even if they unlocked them another way.

Empires with the Wilderness origin must pay an additional 400 Biomass to build or upgrade a fallen empire building.

They cannot be built on Thrall-Worlds or penal colony Penal Colonies.

{{icon|building}} '''Buildings''' are structures that can be constructed on a colony, filling the colony's buildings slots. 6 building slots are available on each colony's [[district|primary district]], and additional building slots are unlocked by [[district specialization]]s. Buildings may be ruined by [[Land warfare|orbital bombardment or collateral damage]]. Buildings that are ruined can be repaired for half of their cost and construction time.

== Building sets ==
Each building belongs to one or more ''building sets''. A building can only be built in a [[district]] that permits one of its building sets and does not exclude any of them, which depends on its [[specialization]]. Changing the specialization of a district may change what buildings are supported and the new specialization's tooltip will display which existing buildings will be retained and which ones will be removed.
* The five general building slots available on all planets, as well as the Urban Expansion specialization, can accept most building sets. The main exceptions are extraction buildings, which can only be built in relevant extraction districts.
* Most specializations can accept an automation building, which produces extra workforce. There are several types with different building sets, each of which has a planet limit of 1. They affect all jobs of types created by the district and its buildings, even if created by other districts or their buildings.
* The Civilian Industry specialization can accept buildings relevant to production of consumer goods, as well as rare resource refineries. Similarly the Heavy Industry specialization can accept buildings relevant to production of alloys. Mixed Industry can accept both.
* Research specializations can accept research buildings relevant to their specialization (all of them if it is a generic Research Enclave). Archives can accept both research and unity buildings, whereas Administrative Hubs can only accept unity buildings.
* Resource districts can accept relevant resource buildings, including output boosters such as the Energy Grid. Notably, Bio-Reactors are considered agriculture buildings, since they alter Farmer jobs to produce energy. Some specializations can accept others, for example Mineral Research Support (mining district specialization) can also accept an Applied Mechanics Institute.
** {{iconify|Agrarian Idyll}} empires can build Agrarian Villages specializations which can accept any "urban" buildings, including energy and mineral extraction.

A total of 21 buildings may be built on a colony. By default the primary district specialization always contains six building slots. Resource districts allow an additional three building slots per specialization.

== Fallen empire buildings ==
Fallen empire buildings are the most efficient buildings in the game. Each one takes 600 days to build or upgrade. They are not converted if the world is conquered by an empire lacking the technology to build them and can also be repaired if ruined.

There are four ways an empire can get access to fallen empire building technologies:
* {{icon|apc}} If Apocalypse is enabled, empires with the {{iconify|Enigmatic Engineering}} ascension perk can draw the technologies as research options. (Up to 4 total researched.)
* {{icon|anr}} If Ancient Relics is enabled, using the Reverse-Engineer Arcane Technology artifact action has a 20% chance (40% with the {{iconify|Archaeo-Engineers}} ascension perk) to grant the ability to build a random fallen empire building once.
* {{icon|tma}} If The Machine Age is enabled, empires with the {{iconify|Cosmogenesis}} ascension perk that have reached the required ambition level can draw the technologies as research options.
* {{icon|bio}} If BioGenesis is enabled, one of the tasks assigned by the Shattered Fragment fallen empires can have a random fallen empire technology as a reward.
Empires with the {{iconify|Cosmogenesis}} ascension perk that accepted the Keepers of Knowledge demand to end the crisis path will no longer be able to build fallen empire buildings, even if they unlocked them another way.

Empires with the {{iconify|Wilderness}} origin must pay an additional 400 {{iconify|Biomass}} to build or upgrade a fallen empire building.

They cannot be built on {{iconify|Thrall-World}}s or {{icon|penal colony}} Penal Colonies.

docs.text:
district Districts represent large areas of development on a planet dedicated towards a particular purpose. Each world can support up to four district sets: a primary district and three secondary district sets. The primary district can have 2 specializations and the secondary districts can only have 1 specialization each. Each district shows a number of district slots that can be in one of 4 states; built, available, blocked or unavailable.

The total number of districts that can be built on a planet is limited by the number of district slots, the base number of which is equal to the colony's planet size, which may then be modified by planetary features, blockers, planet modifiers, or traditions. Effects of each district set stack with each district built, and contribute to the total district effect. The number of mining, generator, and agriculture district slots is further constrained by the deposit features on the planet. Each district increases empire size by a default amount of 0.5.

- Primary districts

Each planet has a primary district that can have 2 specializations. The primary district type depends on empire and planet class and will be converted if the world is terraformed or conquered by an empire which uses a different primary district. The number of districts that can be built is limited only by the number of free district slots on the world. The last primary district on the planet cannot be demolished or replaced.
